title: Blues and Pentatonics
goal: Solo over a twelve-bar blues in A, knowing where the changes are and landing on notes that belong to them.
assumes: You know the open chords and can fret and pick single notes, and you can play eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM. Nothing about scales or blues is assumed. The early Exercises are all in A, on purpose, so that theory is the only new thing; later ones move to other keys.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM

orderRationale: Close to the starting order, with one change of weight. Chord tones arrive in Step 2, before the blues scale, since landing on the right note matters more than knowing an extra one. Call and response is Step 3 because it is the fastest way to make any notes sound like music, and it needs almost no theory. The blues scale and bends both come after the player can land, so neither becomes a thing to sit on. Connecting a second box comes late on purpose: a second box is more notes, and more notes before good choices makes for faster bad solos. Guide tones are Step 9 because they're the most abstract idea here and are easiest once the form is in the ear. Slow blues comes last as it hides nothing.
gradingLimits: Note identity comes from pitch.rs after the take, on single notes, and it has only been tested on synthetic guitars with no band in the signal. So direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade anything with a band behind it; with a microphone and speakers, the band reaches the same input and this is untested. Landing grades look only at the note nearest the landing moment and say nothing of the notes in between. Bends are not measured at all today, so every bend Exercise is self-checked by ear against a fretted reference. Whether a solo is good isn't measured or claimed. Free-playing Exercises are marked either as graded at landings or as practice-only, and no Exercise grades feel.

steps.title: Pentatonic box 1
steps.goal: Play the A minor pentatonic box from memory, find its three A's, and make a first phrase out of it.
steps.why: These five notes are most of the blues and rock you've ever heard. Learning one box well, and knowing which note is the root, gets you playing over a band today. Without the roots, the box is a pattern: with them, it's a map you can navigate.
howTo: First finger stays on fret 5, one finger per fret. The notes are A, C, D, E, G, and every string uses two of them.
Say the note names as you go up, at least the A's: fret 5 on the low E, fret 7 on the D string, fret 5 on the high E.
Let a note ring until the next one starts, and damp strings you aren't using with the side of your picking hand.
steps.payoff: You can play a short phrase over an A7 groove and it sounds like blues straight away.

exercises.title: Box 1, up and down
exercises.purpose: Put the shape in the hand, with every note where it's meant to be.
howTo: Eighth notes, all six strings up and back. Keep a steady, unhurried pace and say the A's out loud.
exercises.coachLine: I'll check the notes after the take. Tempo isn't the point here.

exercises.title: Find the three A's
exercises.purpose: The root is home. Every phrase you make will be judged by your ear against it, so you must be able to find it without looking.
howTo: Low E fret 5, D string fret 7, high E fret 5, then back to the D string. Let each one ring for two beats, and listen to how the same note changes across octaves.
exercises.coachLine: Four right notes in time is all this asks.

exercises.title: A first phrase
exercises.purpose: Six notes and a rest, with a beginning and an end. Hearing yourself play a phrase rather than a scale is the payoff of this Step.
howTo: Top string down to the D string, ending on A. Leave the silence in the second bar alone: it is part of the phrase.
exercises.coachLine: It's a short one. I'll say if the notes were right, and the rest is your ear's job.

exercises.title: Free in the box, over A7
exercises.purpose: Your first time making up notes over a band. Stay inside the box, where every note you play will at least belong.
howTo: Any notes, any order, no wrong answers inside these frets. Leave gaps. The written line is one example of how it might go, not a target.
exercises.coachLine: Inside the box is all I'm checking here. Choosing well is a later Step.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Landing on chord tones
steps.goal: Choose where a phrase ends: on a note that belongs to the chord the band is playing at that moment.
steps.why: This is the single biggest step from playing scales to playing changes. A wrong-sounding note is mostly a note that stopped in the wrong place. You can play anything in the box on the way; if the note on the first beat of the bar belongs to the chord, the phrase sounds as if you meant it.
howTo: Over A7 the chord tones are A, C#, E, G. Box 1 holds A, E and G of those. Its C is the blue third: it rubs against the band's C#, on purpose, and it is not a landing note yet.
D7 is D, F#, A, C. E7 is E, G#, B, D. From box 1 you have D, A and C over D7, and E and D over E7.
Aim for the note first, then get there. Decide on it a beat early.
steps.payoff: The same box suddenly follows the chords, and you can hear when you got it right.

exercises.title: A on every downbeat
exercises.purpose: Written phrases that land on A at every bar line. The feel of arriving, before it becomes a choice.
howTo: Two beats of A, then a small move and back. Land on the next bar line as if it were the point of the whole bar, because it is.
exercises.coachLine: The written notes are the bar here, and they all land on A.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Land on A, E or G
exercises.purpose: Your choice now, but only at the landing. Anything goes in between, and the one thing graded is the note on beat 1.
howTo: Over the A7 groove, make a little phrase that ends on beat 1 of the next bar, on A, E or G. C does not count yet, even though it sounds bluesy.
exercises.coachLine: I only listen on beat 1 of each bar. Play whatever you like in between.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.feedbackNote: Knowing at the next bar line whether you landed is the lesson. It needs the per-bar pitch slice, which is not built (audit, section 3). Until then it reports after the take.

exercises.title: A7 to D7
exercises.purpose: The first change. The same A that was home a bar ago is still a chord tone over D7, and D is right beside it.
howTo: Two bars of A7, two of D7. Land on any chord tone on each beat 1. Over D7, try D, then A, then C.
exercises.coachLine: Beat 1 of each bar is all I judge. The change is what this one trains.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.feedbackNote: The same per-bar readout as the last Exercise, for the same reason, and it reports after the take until that is built.

exercises.title: A7, D7, E7 in four bars
exercises.purpose: All three chords of a blues, one bar each, with a written line that hits the root at every change.
howTo: The line lands on A, D, E and A. Play it until those landings are obvious, then try your own in the same place.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes here, and they are the right ones if they land where the chart does.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Call and response
steps.goal: Hear a phrase, play one back, and leave space: the conversation that blues is built on.
steps.why: Blues is a conversation, and most beginners only ever talk. Answering a phrase teaches you to phrase in lengths a listener can follow, and it forces you to stop playing. It does more for how you sound, per minute, than any scale you can learn.
howTo: Listen to the whole call before you play. Don't start planning your answer until it has finished.
Keep your answer about as long as the call. Two bars of question deserves two bars of answer.
Silence is a note. A bar with nothing in it is a decision, and a good one.
steps.payoff: You can trade two-bar phrases with the app and it sounds like a conversation.

exercises.title: Echo
exercises.purpose: The app plays a two-bar phrase; you play it back, note for note, by ear. Exercising the ear is what this is for.
howTo: Try not to look at the tab. Sing the phrase back before you play it, once, if you can.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I can say if the echo had the right notes. It's fine to take a few tries.
exercises.feedbackNote: The app has to play the call: the synth voice can do that, and the Exercise format carries it as a guide part, but nothing wires that up yet.

exercises.title: Same rhythm, your notes
exercises.purpose: Keep the rhythm of the call and choose new notes in the box. A lot of a phrase's identity is rhythm, as you'll hear when you change only the pitches.
howTo: The written notes are just an example. Hold on to the rhythm and pick anything from box 1.
exercises.coachLine: I can time your notes against the rhythm and check that they stayed in the box. Which ones you chose is yours.

exercises.title: Two bars on, two bars off
exercises.purpose: Over the band, play for two bars and then stop for two. Most players find the stopping much harder.
howTo: Anything from the box for two bars, then hands off. Count the two silent bars out loud if you have to.
exercises.coachLine: I check that the rests stay empty, and that notes stay in the box. On a microphone the band can land in those rests, so use direct input.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Free trade
exercises.purpose: The app calls, you answer however you like. This is the one that sounds most like playing blues with someone. Ungraded, because a good answer isn't something the app can judge.
howTo: Answer with whatever comes. Try once with very few notes and once with a lot, and hear which you like better.
exercises.coachLine: No marks on this one. Enjoy it, and listen back if you recorded.

steps.difficultyException: The note rate falls because half of these bars are silence; listening and leaving space is the new demand, which is not a rate.

steps.title: The blues scale and the blue notes
steps.goal: Add the flat five as a note to pass through, and hear the third move from C to C#.
steps.why: Two notes turn a scale into the blues. The flat five, Eb in A, sounds wrong on its own and wonderful on its way somewhere else. The blue third, C rubbing against the chord's C#, is the tension the whole style runs on. You've been playing the C already; now you'll hear what it's doing.
howTo: The A blues scale is A, C, D, Eb, E, G. Eb lives at fret 6 on the A string and fret 8 on the G string in this box.
Don't park on the Eb. Slide or walk through it on your way to D or E.
To resolve the blue third, hammer from C to C# with your first and second fingers on the G string. Bend C a little toward C# as a variation.
steps.payoff: One extra note, and suddenly the lick sounds like the blues rather than a rock scale.

exercises.title: A blues scale, box 1
exercises.purpose: The box with its one new note, so you can find the Eb without thinking.
howTo: Eighth notes up and down. The Eb gives the A string three frets in a row: first, second and third fingers.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes after the take, the same as before.

exercises.title: Passing, not parking
exercises.purpose: A lick with the flat five exactly where it belongs: on the way from D to E, and back from E to D.
howTo: Play it straight, then again with a slight swing. The Eb is the shortest note in your thinking: it never lands.
exercises.coachLine: The Eb goes by quickly. I can check the note after the take, and how it sounds is what you're listening for.

exercises.title: From C to C#
exercises.purpose: The sound of the blues in one small move: from minor to major third, landing on the chord's real third.
howTo: Pick C at fret 5 on the G string and hammer on to fret 6. C# belongs to A7, so this is the first time you have really played the chord's own third.
exercises.coachLine: A quiet hammer won't count against you, and pick it if you prefer.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Land clean, one blue note a phrase
exercises.purpose: Free playing with a rule: a single flat five or blue third per phrase, and a chord tone on beat 1. It stops the new notes from taking over.
howTo: Only beat 1 is graded. The blue note is a rule you keep yourself.
exercises.coachLine: I can check beat 1. The rule about blue notes is on your honour.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Following the 12-bar
steps.goal: Know where you are in the form without counting bars, and hear the turnaround coming.
steps.why: Losing your place is the number one bedroom problem. The form is twelve bars: four of A7, two of D7, two of A7, then E7, D7, A7, E7. Once it's in your ear you stop counting and start anticipating, and that's when solos start to have a shape. Playing the bass line is the fastest way there: you can't get lost when you're the one playing it.
howTo: Count the form as 4 + 4 + 4, as the Jam timeline does. Each four is a sentence.
Listen for the bar 9 change to E7. It's the moment the form really moves.
Bars 11 and 12 are the turnaround: they exist only to bring you back to the top.
steps.payoff: You hear the changes coming, and you can play a turnaround that brings the chorus home.

exercises.title: One root per bar, all twelve
exercises.purpose: As simple as it gets: a whole note on the root of each bar's chord, all the way through the form.
howTo: A on the low E string, D and E on the A string. Hear each move before you play it. Don't count: listen for the band's change.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve notes, right notes, on the bar. If you got lost, the band will tell you first.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The boogie line
exercises.purpose: A walking shuffle line through the whole form, so you're playing the changes rather than following them. It is the same shape moved to three roots.
howTo: Root, third, fifth, sixth, flat seven, and back. Swing it: long, short, long, short. It's a stretch from fret 5 to 9 on one string, so let the hand move.
exercises.coachLine: A lot of notes and long form, and I'll report them after the take. Getting all the way through is the win.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A turnaround
exercises.purpose: Bars 11 and 12: a descending line over the A7, ending on the E7 that sends you back to the top. Every chorus you play will need one.
howTo: The G on the B string stays while E, Eb, D and C# step down under it. Then land on E and the G# below, and you're home.
exercises.coachLine: Two bars, and I'll check the notes after the take. Play it until you can do it without thinking.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Land on every change, all twelve bars
exercises.purpose: A whole free chorus. You choose everything, and the only thing graded is the note on beat 1 at each chord change.
howTo: Six landings in twelve bars. Know the next chord before you get to it. If you lose the form, wait and rejoin at bar 5 or bar 9.
exercises.coachLine: Only the changes count, which is six moments. Everything else in the chorus is yours.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.feedbackNote: A per-bar strip helps most here, and needs the same per-bar pitch slice. Reports after the take until then.

steps.title: Bends that land
steps.goal: Bend a note up to an exact pitch and hold it there, on a chord tone.
steps.why: A bend is the guitar's voice, and it's only expressive when it arrives. A bend that stops short sounds like a mistake in a way a wrong note often doesn't. The way to learn it is simple, and it's old: play the note you want, then bend up to it and compare.
howTo: Bend with three fingers on the string, ring finger on the note. Push from the wrist, as if turning a door handle, rather than from the fingers alone.
Play the target first. Then bend until there's no wobble left between what you hear and what you remember.
Bends aren't graded: the app doesn't measure them today, so your ear is the judge on every one of these. Keep your strings fresh: old strings make this much harder.
steps.payoff: A bent note that sits exactly on the band's chord tone and sings.

exercises.title: Target first, then bend
exercises.purpose: Play the note, then bend up to it from a whole tone below: E, then D bent to E; A, then G bent to A; D, then C bent to D.
howTo: Two beats on the target, two beats on the bend. Hold the top of the bend without moving it. Use your ear and nothing else.
exercises.coachLine: I can't measure how far a bend goes, so your ear decides this one. Compare it to the note you just played.

notes: A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Does the top of the bend match the note you played just before, with no wobble between them?
Could you hold the top of the bend for the full two beats?

exercises.title: The half-step bend to C#
exercises.purpose: From C up to the chord's own third. It's a small, exact bend and it's the classic blues sound, moving from the blue third to the major third over A7.
howTo: Fret 9 on the top string is your C#: play that first. Then fret 8 bent a half step. A half step feels like almost nothing, which is why it often overshoots.
exercises.coachLine: Half-step bends tend to go sharp, and it takes your ear to catch it.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Did the bend reach the C# you played first, and stop there rather than going past it?

exercises.title: Bends on the beat
exercises.purpose: A bend needs to arrive on time too, and that part the app can help with: it can tell whether each bend was picked when it was meant to be.
howTo: One bend on each beat of the first bar, then let it go. Start the bend as you pick, and reach the top quickly. Your ear still decides if it landed.
exercises.coachLine: I can only tell you the bends started on time. How far they travelled, you judge.

notes: A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Did each bend reach its note, on your ear?

exercises.title: Bends that land on the chord
exercises.purpose: A bent note on each change, and each one lands on a tone of that chord. E over A7, A over D7, E over E7 and C# over A7.
howTo: Hear the target. The bend in bar 4 is the half step, and the others are whole steps. Each fill stays in the box.
exercises.coachLine: I can't measure any of the bends here, so this is one to record and listen back to.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: On a recording, does each bend sit in tune with the band's chord?
Did you reach the top of each bend before beat 2?

steps.difficultyException: Bends are slow on purpose, so the rate falls. Pitch control by ear is the demand, which the metric only partly counts.

steps.title: Question and answer phrases
steps.goal: Write phrases that ask and phrases that resolve, and build a twelve-bar chorus from them.
steps.why: A phrase that ends on the root sounds finished. A phrase that ends anywhere else sounds like a question. Knowing that gives you the shape of almost every blues vocal ever sung: say it, say it again, then answer it. It's the point where you stop stringing licks together and start saying something.
howTo: A question often ends on G or C, and an answer ends on A. Start both the same way and only change the ending: the listener hears the relationship.
Blues lyric form is A, A, B: the same line twice, then the reply. Use that form on the guitar.
Over D7, the same line sounds different, which is why repeating it doesn't get boring.
steps.payoff: A twelve-bar chorus that has a beginning, a middle and an end, and uses very few notes.

exercises.title: A question and its answer
exercises.purpose: The same start twice, and two different endings. Hear what one note does: G asks and A answers.
howTo: Bars 1 and 2 are the question, ending on G. Bars 3 and 4 are the answer, ending on A. Let each ending note ring.
exercises.coachLine: I'll check the written notes after the take. Whether it sounds like a question is your ear's call.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: You write the answer
exercises.purpose: The app asks. You answer with anything you like, ending on A at the start of bar 4. It's graded on that one note, and nothing else.
howTo: Listen to the question, make up your answer, and make sure it finishes on an A. Try the fret 7 A on the D string first.
exercises.coachLine: One landing is all I check: the A at the start of bar 4. The rest of your answer is yours.
exercises.feedbackNote: One note per take, so after-the-take is enough, and it needs no new runtime thread.

exercises.title: A, A, B over twelve bars
exercises.purpose: The same line over A7 and over D7, then an answer over E7 and D7. A blues chorus, written out, with about seven notes to a phrase.
howTo: Bars 1 and 5 start the same, and the band changes under you. That change is the magic. Bars 9 and 10 are the reply. Rest everywhere it says.
exercises.coachLine: A lot of silence in this one. The rests count as much as the notes in how it sounds, even though I only check the notes.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your own A, A, B
exercises.purpose: A whole chorus of your own in that form, which nothing grades. Say something, repeat it and answer it.
howTo: Make up the A phrase on the spot and repeat it over D7. Don't plan the B. Record it, and be kind to yourself about what comes out.
exercises.coachLine: No marks on this one. If you want a view, listen back to it tomorrow.

steps.difficultyException: Long notes and rests lower the rate on purpose: fewer notes, chosen more carefully, is what this Step teaches, and the rate can't count choosing.

steps.title: Connecting box 1 and box 2
steps.goal: Move between the first two pentatonic boxes through shared notes, without the seam showing.
steps.why: One box keeps you in a cage. The way out isn't to learn all five at once: it's to find one door. Box 2 uses the same five notes, a little higher, and the D and G strings give you a slide from one box into the other. That's enough to change how your solos sound, because a higher note on the same scale is a whole new emotion in the phrase.
howTo: Box 2 starts at fret 7 or 8: on the G string it is frets 7 and 9, on the B string frets 8 and 10.
The door is a slide on the G string from D at fret 7 up to E at fret 9. Slide with your third finger and you land in position in box 2.
Box 1 and box 2 are the same notes. A on the D string, fret 7, is the same in both, and you've already found it.
steps.payoff: Your lick climbs out of the box, reaches a new high note, and comes home again.

exercises.title: Box 2, up and down
exercises.purpose: The new shape on its own: the same notes in a new layout.
howTo: Eighth notes, up and back. Say the A's again: fret 7 on the D string and fret 10 on the B string.
exercises.coachLine: Same bar as box 1. I'll check the notes after the take.

exercises.title: The door: slide up, come home
exercises.purpose: One lick, from box 1 into box 2 and back. Sliding D to E on the G string and A to G on the B string are the two doors.
howTo: Slide on the G string to reach E. Top note A at fret 10 on the B string, then slide back to G. Pick each slide's first note only.
exercises.coachLine: A slid-to note can be too quiet for me. If I miss one, that's on the listening, so trust your ear there.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.

exercises.title: Four bars, both boxes
exercises.purpose: A longer phrase that uses box 2 for its high point and box 1 for its landing. The shape of the line goes up and comes home, which is what makes it sound like a solo.
howTo: Bars 1 and 2 climb, bar 3 sits high, and bar 4 comes home to A. Take the slides slowly at first.
exercises.coachLine: Notes after the take. Get the slides clean, and the rest usually follows.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Land in either box
exercises.purpose: Free playing across both boxes with the landings still graded: more room to move, same discipline.
howTo: Land on chord tones on beat 1, using whichever box you're in. E on the G string, fret 9, is a good new landing over A7 and E7 alike.
exercises.coachLine: Beat 1 of each bar is all I judge, in either box.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Guide tones through the changes
steps.goal: Hear and play the thirds and sevenths that make each chord what it is, and move between them by half steps.
steps.why: If you only play two notes per chord, these are the two. The third and seventh of a dominant chord tell the ear exactly what's happening, and from one chord to the next they barely move: G falls a half step to F#, C# falls to C. Play that, and the changes appear in a single line with no band at all. It's the moment theory turns into something you can hear.
howTo: A7's guide tones are C# and G. D7's are F# and C. E7's are G# and D.
G to F# (A7 to D7) and C# to C (A7 to D7) are half steps. E7's G# is the odd one out: go up a tone from F# on the B string.
Sing the line. If you can sing it, you can play over the changes.
steps.payoff: A single slow line that spells the whole twelve-bar form without any other notes.

exercises.title: The seventh-and-third line, on the B string
exercises.purpose: One note per bar, all on one string: G over A7, F# over D7, G# over E7. These are the sounds that make the changes obvious.
howTo: Whole notes at frets 8, 7 and 9, in that order as the chart asks. Let the band's chord move under you and hear the note fit.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve notes, and I'll check that each is the right one for its chord.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The other line
exercises.purpose: C# over A7, C over D7, G# over E7: the other guide tone for each chord, a lower line that moves by half steps too.
howTo: Frets 6 and 5 on the G string and fret 6 on the D string. Compare it with the last line: the same form, a different colour.
exercises.coachLine: The same check, on a new line. Once both are easy, the next Exercise joins them.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Both guide tones, every chord
exercises.purpose: Two half notes per bar through the form: third, then seventh. The chord's identity comes through with nothing else played.
howTo: Stay in fifth position. Fingers fall on these two strings and barely have to move at each change, which is the whole point.
exercises.coachLine: It's slow, but every note counts. I'll check each one after the take.

exercises.title: Guide tones with a pentatonic fill
exercises.purpose: Land on a guide tone on beat 1, then fill with the box. It's the sound of a player who is really hearing the changes.
howTo: The fill stays in box 1. Note how the C# and G# stand out against the band's chord, because that's what they're for.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes on this one, and I'll check them after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Land on guide tones, all twelve bars
exercises.purpose: A free chorus again, now aiming only for thirds and sevenths at each change. It's the hardest landing in the Path, and the most rewarding.
howTo: Six changes in twelve bars. Pick a guide tone for each ahead of time, and everything else is free.
exercises.coachLine: Six moments again, but only a third or a seventh counts now. Don't worry about the notes in between.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.feedbackNote: Same need for the per-bar pitch slice as the earlier landings. Reports after the take until then.

steps.difficultyException: One or two notes a bar, so the rate falls right down. Hearing the harmony is the demand here, and it is the most abstract idea on the Path.

steps.title: Slow blues
steps.goal: Play a full chorus at a slow tempo, where every note you play is on display.
steps.why: At 60 BPM there's nowhere to hide and nothing to run to. Everything in this Path is a tool for this moment: chord tones to land on, bends that arrive, questions and answers, and rests. Slow blues is the hardest thing on the Path, and it isn't because of the notes.
howTo: Feel the triplets under the beat: each beat has three pulses, and the drummer plays them on the hat.
Play less than you think. Let a held note ring through a chord change if it still fits, and hear how it changes.
Use vibrato only once a note has landed, not to find it.
steps.payoff: Twelve slow bars that sound like a blues player, with the space to prove it.

exercises.title: A written slow chorus
exercises.purpose: A full twelve bars, written, with bends and blue notes in place, to show how little it takes. Learn it, and take it apart.
howTo: Rest where it rests, and hold notes for their full length. The bends need your ear, since the app doesn't measure them.
exercises.coachLine: This one has bends and long notes that I can't really judge, so it's on your own ear. Record it.

notes: Hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides may be too quiet to detect. An unheard hammer-on or pull-off costs nothing. An unheard slid-to note still counts as missed today, so the bar here allows for it.
With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
A bend is one attack. The app can time it; it does not measure how far it travelled.

selfCheck: Does each held note sit against the band's chord?
On a recording, do the bends reach their notes?

exercises.title: Your slow chorus, landing on the changes
exercises.purpose: Your notes, the same form, graded only on the six landings. The written chorus is an example of one way it might go.
howTo: At this tempo you have plenty of time to choose. Land on a chord tone at each change and leave a gap after it.
exercises.coachLine: Only the changes count here, six in the chorus. I'd rather hear fewer notes.

exercises.title: Play less
exercises.purpose: A chorus with most of its bars empty. Rests are graded here, as a way of saying they matter. The rule: if the written example rests, you rest too.
howTo: Seven bars of music and five of silence. Listen to the band in those bars, since it's worth hearing.
exercises.coachLine: I check that the empty bars stay empty, on direct input. On a microphone the band gets in the way of that.

exercises.title: A free chorus, nobody's counting
exercises.purpose: Play a slow chorus of your own, the way you'd play it for a friend. There's nothing to pass, and the app says so. It's the point of the whole Path.
howTo: Record it if you'd like to hear it. Otherwise, close your eyes.
exercises.coachLine: No marks and no report. This one is for you.

levels.title: Beginner: one box, and where to land
levels.summary: One pentatonic box, landing on notes that belong to the chord, and leaving space. All in A, so the theory is the only new thing.

startHereIf: You can play eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM.
You don't yet know box 1 from memory, or you know it and can't make it sound like a phrase.
You couldn't name the notes of A7 yet.

warmups.title: A lick around the chords
warmups.purpose: A short shuffle lick in box 1, moved to follow i, IV, V and back. A new key and a new lick each time, so your hands wake up and your ears do too.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Swing it. Shift at the bar line and let the chord tell you where you are.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

levels.title: Intermediate: the form and the voice
levels.summary: The blues scale, all twelve bars, bends that land, and phrases that ask and answer.

startHereIf: You can play box 1 from memory, up and down, at 80 BPM eighths.
Over A7, D7 and E7 you can land on a chord tone on beat 1 for four bars running.
You get lost in the twelve-bar form, or your solos run together with no shape to them.

warmups.title: A boogie line in a new key
warmups.purpose: A walking shuffle line round I, IV, V and back, in a key you didn't play yesterday. It's a warm-up and ear training at once.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Root, third, fifth, sixth, flat seven and back. Let the hand move.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

levels.title: Advanced: more neck, more harmony, less noise
levels.summary: A second box, guide tones through the changes, and slow blues with nothing to hide behind.

startHereIf: You can follow all 12 bars without losing your place.
You can bend a whole tone up to pitch by ear, and hold it there.
Your phrases work, and you're stuck in one box playing the same notes over every chord.

warmups.title: Through both boxes
warmups.purpose: A four-bar line from box 1 into box 2 and home again, in a different key each time. The slide on the G string is what gets warmed up.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Take the slide slowly and let the line rise and come home.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.
